hook.text: Entities never live alone. Customers matter because they place orders. And orders matter because they contain products.

verbs.text: So if entities are the nouns, relationships are the verbs. And a good one reads like a sentence. Customer places order says more than customer has order.

rows.text: Zoom in, and that line is really rows linking to rows. Ada's row links to orders one oh one and one oh two. Grace's, to one oh three.

key.text: Postgres keeps each link as a key. Every order just carries its customer's id.

idea.text: The relationship is the idea... and the foreign key is how the database holds on to it.

many-in.text: But a bare line leaves a big question open. How many?

both.text: That's cardinality, and you ask it both ways. One customer, how many orders? Zero, one, or many.

other.text: One order, how many customers? Exactly one.

one-to-many.text: That's one-to-many, and the key sits on the many side. Two orders, both storing Ada's id.

ends.text: Crow's-foot notation draws those answers right onto the line. Every end gets two marks.

max.text: Next to the box is the most. A bar means one, and a crow's foot means many.

min.text: Farther out is the least. A circle means zero, and a bar means one.

one.text: Two bars, exactly one. A profile belongs to one user.

zero-or-one.text: A bar and a circle, zero or one. An employee gets one parking pass, at most.

one-or-many.text: A foot and a bar, one or many. An order holds at least one item.

zero-or-many.text: A foot and a circle, zero or many. A customer might not have ordered yet.

m2m.text: And feet at both ends? That's many-to-many, like students and courses.

schema.text: And those marks change the schema. Many devices per employee? Then device rows can share an employee id.

badge.text: But one badge, at most? Then no employee id can show up twice.

reject.text: Give Ada a second badge... and Postgres says NO.

translate.text: It never sees your picture. You translate it, into keys and constraints.

shop.text: So let's read one, properly. A little shop: customers, orders, order items, products. Read each line as a sentence.

s1.text: One customer places zero or many orders.

s2.text: One order contains one or many order items.

s3.text: One product appears in zero or many order items.

wrong.text: If a sentence sounds wrong to the business, the diagram needs work.

joins.text: Then follow the keys. Each one is a join, so the diagram maps out the query. Ada, her order, its lines, their products.

next.text: And each line lands on exactly one row, because every row has a name nothing else shares... a key.
